template.title: Idea Stage
template.subtitle: Check whether the idea makes sense
template.intro: Reduce uncertainty and find the gaps in your own idea. Check who your idea can help, what problem it solves for those people and whether it can make money.
general.title: General validation
general.intro: The foundation for every idea, no matter what you're building or who you're selling to.
general/zdefiniuj-problem.title: Define the problem
general/zdefiniuj-problem.guide_body:
Describe a specific situation
Start with what causes someone difficulty. “People waste time” is too broad. “A shop owner compares several files every Friday to work out what to order” already lets you picture the situation and find a person to talk to.
In the problem field, describe what this person wants to do, when they try to do it and what gets in their way. If you see the word “case” in the form, it means exactly such a specific instance. Avoid writing “no app”, because that imposes the solution in advance. The obstacle can be, for example, scattered information, difficulty finding help or a complicated task.
If you're relying on your own experience, give an example. If you don't know something yet, mark it “assumption” or “to be checked”. Don't make up data to fill in a field.
Name the person and how they work today
Pick a group whose members can be recognized by traits related to the problem. Instead of “entrepreneurs” you can write “owners of small online shops who order stock themselves”. Add age, gender or city only when they matter for the difficulty you're describing.
Then describe how such a person copes today. They may use a program, keep notes, hire help or put up with the inconvenience. If they do nothing, it's worth asking later why. Doing nothing can mean a small need, but also a lack of time, money or an available way to get help.
Separate the obstacle from its effects
The obstacle is, e.g., having to compare three separate files. The effect is the time spent on it or a mistake in the order. Write down both, so you know what you want to improve and why anyone would care about it.
Give numbers when you have grounds to use them: “according to the interviewee, about an hour a week”. If you only suspect that mistakes cause losses, write it down as a question to check. Don't present possible consequences as something that has already been observed.
Rate importance and urgency
The 1–5 slider helps organize your current assessment. You can take 1 to mean a minor inconvenience, 3 a clear difficulty and 5 serious consequences or a blocked important task. Ratings 2 and 4 are in between. That's the working meaning of the scale in this exercise, with no threshold that passes the idea.
Urgency answers a different question: how quickly does something need to be done about it? A problem can be painful but only appear in a few months. On the need-for-a-solution slider, consider whether the person can calmly wait or has to act now. Later compare your own rating with examples from the interviews. A high rating alone doesn't prove readiness to buy.
Build the problem statement from five fields
Fill in, in order: who, what they're trying to do, in what situation, what gets in the way and what the effect is. You'll get a sentence following the pattern: “[Who] are trying to [do what] [in what situation], but [obstacle], so [effect]”. Fix the wording if the automatically assembled text sounds clumsy.
Example: “Owners of small online shops are trying to work out what to order during their weekly restocking, but the data is scattered across several files, so comparing the information by hand takes them a lot of time”.
After this point you have a problem description, a specific recipient and an initial assessment of how much the difficulty matters. The “final definition” in the form is a summary for now. You can improve it after the interviews.
Paul Graham, How to Get Startup Ideas. Basis: looking for the problems of specific recipients and recognizing a strong need.
Paul Graham, Before the Startup. Basis: getting to know users and their problems at the start of the work.
Describe the problem and where it occurs
general/zdefiniuj-problem/opisz-problem/: What currently doesn't work, who does this problem affect and why?
The more specific, the better. “People waste time” is too broad — describe a specific person and a specific situation.
Describe the specific situation, moment and context in which the problem occurs.
When exactly does it happen? Once a week, with every order, at the end of the month?
general/zdefiniuj-problem/przykladowy-uz: Describe the person or organization the problem affects.
Role, situation, industry — whatever matters for your idea. Instead of “entrepreneurs” write “owners of small online shops”.
How does this person deal with the problem today?
What products, services, processes, workarounds or manual solutions do they use? If they do nothing — that's an answer too.
general/zdefiniuj-problem/gdzie-nie-dzia: Name the specific problems with the current way of doing things.
Wasted time, costs, mistakes, frustration, inconvenience. Give numbers when you have grounds: “according to the interviewee, about an hour a week”.
Lost revenue, risk, wasted resources, missed opportunities. Separate the obstacle itself from its effects.
general/zdefiniuj-problem/waznosc-proble: How serious is this problem for the person it affects?
1 is a minor inconvenience, 3 a clear difficulty, 5 serious consequences.
How urgently does it need solving?
This is a different question from seriousness. A problem can be painful but only appear in a few months.
It has to be solved immediately
general/zdefiniuj-problem/ostateczna-def: Build the problem into one sentence from the earlier answers. Write about the difficulty, not about your product.
Build the problem statement from five fields.
Read the finished sentence out loud. If it sounds artificial or too general — fix the fields it was built from.

Owners of small online shops are trying to work out what to order during their weekly restocking, but the data is scattered across several files, so they lose an hour a week and order too little stock.
What are they trying to do?
What makes it hard for them?
general/hipoteza-rozwiazania.title: Define the solution hypothesis
general/hipoteza-rozwiazania.guide_body:
A “hypothesis” is an assumption you intend to check. Here you'll describe how you want to help the chosen person and what has to hold true for this idea to make sense. At this stage a short description and the scope of the simplest test are enough.
Explain what you offer and to whom
Answer the four questions in the form in plain words: what the solution does, who it's for, what problem it solves and what result it gives. It's good if someone outside your team can picture how it would be used after reading it.
Example: “A tool for owners of small online shops that combines sales and stock data into one list of suggested orders. It's meant to shorten the weekly stock check”. Shortening the time is, for now, a promise to be checked.
Show how the user gets the benefit
Describe a short sequence of events: what the user provides or does, what happens with it next and what they get. In the example, the owner hands over the files, the tool compares the data and they get a list of products to check before ordering.
A feature is the ability to do something, e.g. load a file. A benefit is what a person gains from it, e.g. less manual copying. For the question about the most important action, name the action needed for this benefit. Creating an account alone usually doesn't give it yet.
Limit the first version
List the features or actions needed to check the main promise. For each one ask: “Can I still check whether I'm helping the user without it?”. If so, put it off for later.
In the example, these are enough: accepting the files, comparing the information and preparing the list. Custom colors, a referral program or detailed statistics can wait. You can do part of the work by hand at first, as long as you clearly explain to the participant how the test works.
MVP is the abbreviation for the first simple version someone can use and get the basic benefit from. In this point you decide its scope. A picture or a presentation can help explain the idea, but they don't yet show whether a working product solves the problem. For a device, a sketch alone won't check its technical performance.
Write down why the idea might work
Complete the sentence: “I assume that [who] will use [what] to [achieve what]”. For example: “I assume that owners of small shops will use a list of suggested orders to restock faster”.
Then list the most important assumptions. Look for things that could turn out wrong and force you into a big change. In our example these are: owners can share the necessary data; the prepared list helps them order; the time saved is worth the proposed price to them.
Choose what you'll check first
For each assumption, consider how little you know about it and what happens if it's wrong. Pick the one that is both important and poorly understood. Write it down as a specific statement, e.g. “Shop owners will agree to hand over the files needed for the test”. “People will like the idea” isn't precise enough.
Keep the remaining assumptions on the list. If the most important unknown concerns, e.g., how a device works, conversations with customers won't settle it. Note that you need a separate technical check.
After this point you have an understandable description of the solution, its essential scope and one assumption to check first.
general/hipoteza-rozwiazania.guide_sourc: Michael Seibel, How to Plan an MVP. Basis: limiting the first version to the basic benefit and learning from its use. The link leads to a summary and a recording of the lecture.

Kevin Hale, How to Evaluate Startup Ideas. Basis: an idea as a set of assumptions about the problem, the solution and the reasons it would succeed. The link leads to a summary and a recording of the lecture.
Paul Graham, Do Things that Don't Scale. Basis: being able to do part of the work by hand at the start.
general/hipoteza-rozwiazania/wersja-mini: List the absolutely essential features needed to test the product, service or process.
For each one ask: “can I still check whether I'm helping the user without it?”. If so — cut it.
Accepting the files · Comparing the information · Preparing the order list
general/hipoteza-rozwiazania/dlaczego-sk: This is the sentence you'll be checking in conversations with people. The more specific it is, the easier it is to disprove or confirm.
I assume that {kto} will use {czego} to {po-co}.
What has to hold true for your idea to have a chance of working?
Pick the assumptions which, if they don't hold, will force you to change the idea. The rest isn't critical.
general/hipoteza-rozwiazania/zalozenie-d: Which assumption is the riskiest and most important?
This is the thing everything else depends on. You'll deal with it first.
general/konkurencja.title: Check how others solve this problem
general/konkurencja.guide_body:
Here you'll check what options your future customer has today. A search engine, the websites of existing products and user reviews will come in handy. You don't need an extensive report. Collect information that will help you compare specific ways of dealing with the problem.
Find products and other ways of doing things
Search by the task or the difficulty, e.g. “how to plan stock orders”, “stock replenishment software” or “too much time spent on warehouse checks”. Also check the names of tools you know from previous work. If it helps, repeat the search in another language.
List three similar products or services and add links. Separately note other ways of doing things: your own spreadsheet, a piece of paper, the work of an extra person or ordering by gut feeling. If fewer than three products came up, write down the results and the places you searched. Don't add dissimilar companies just to make up the number.
Collect comparable information
For each solution, answer the questions in the form. First check the product page, the description of how it works and the pricing. Note the recipients, the problem solved, the promised result and a few key features.
Write down the price together with its terms: per month or per year, per person or for the whole company, for which capabilities. “Price from $10” says little without this information. If the amount is only available after talking to a salesperson, write “custom quote”. For manual methods, include the time or effort, even when there's no fee for software. Keep the link and the date you checked.
Read the praise and the complaints
Look at reviews, groups related to the topic and discussions about the product. Write down what people value and what they struggle with. Look for specific situations: “every week I copy the data over”, “I can't set it up myself”, “this feature saves me an hour”.
A single review is a lead. A recurring remark deserves further checking, but it still doesn't tell you how common the problem is among all users. Pay attention to the date and the product version. Don't pick only the comments that fit your idea.
If you notice an overlooked group, describe it specifically: “owners of one-person shops without IT help”. A missing feature in a product doesn't automatically mean anyone wants it added. You can ask about it in later conversations.
Compare the idea and the cost of switching
Say what you plan to do differently, who it should help and how the proposed price compares. Separate what a competitor already offers from what you're only promising to build. Avoid generalities like “better quality”. Be specific, e.g. “the user will get the list without copying data by hand”.
Also write down the advantages of the current solution: familiarity, reliability, existing data or technical support. A person may stay with a less convenient way if switching to a new one takes a lot of work. Ask what would have to make up for it. In the example, saving a dozen or so minutes may not be enough if preparing the files for the new tool takes an hour.
If you can't find any competition
Check other names for the problem and ask people from the chosen group how they cope. Write down possible explanations for the lack of products: the need is small, people use a workaround, the solution is hard to build or nobody has developed this idea yet. Next to the explanation you choose, add a way to check it, e.g. a conversation with a recipient or with someone who knows the technology.
After this point you have a short comparison, links to the information and an idea of what could persuade a customer to switch. The presence or absence of competitors alone doesn't decide whether it's worth continuing.
general/konkurencja.guide_sources.0: Paul Graham, How to Get Startup Ideas, the Competition section. Basis: looking for needs overlooked by existing solutions.
general/konkurencja.guide_sources.1: Eric Migicovsky, How to Talk to Users. Basis: learning about the ways of doing things people use and their limitations. The link leads to a summary and a recording of the lecture.
general/konkurencja/znajdz-rozwiazania/p: List three products or services that solve a similar problem.
They don't have to be identical. The point is what your recipient reaches for today.
general/konkurencja/znajdz-rozwiazania/o: What other ways do people use to deal with this problem?
They do something by hand, ask someone for help, use Excel or simply put up with the inconvenience. That's competition too.
general/konkurencja/opisz-rozwiazania/ja: How do they solve the problem and what does the user gain from it?
general/konkurencja/opisz-rozwiazania/ce: How much do they cost and what do you pay for?
If you don't know the price, write “no public pricing” — that's information too.
general/konkurencja/opisz-rozwiazania/fu: What are their most important features or traits?
general/konkurencja/opinie-uzytkownikow/: I've read reviews, comments or discussions about these solutions.
Reviews in app stores, forum threads, comments on Reddit and in groups — that's where people tell the truth.
What do they complain about and what are they missing?
This is the most valuable part. A gap in someone else's product is your chance.
Does any group of people have needs these solutions don't meet? Which ones?
Links to the reviews you found
They'll come in handy later, when you come back to these conclusions.
general/konkurencja/porownaj.title: Compare your idea
general/konkurencja/porownaj/inaczej.que: What do you want to do differently from existing solutions?
general/konkurencja/porownaj/ci-sami-lud: Do you want to help the same people? If not — whom?
general/konkurencja/porownaj/cena.questi: How does your planned price compare with theirs?
general/konkurencja/porownaj/cena.help: If you don't know it yet, write “to be decided” — you'll come back to it in point 5.
general/konkurencja/porownaj/przewagi.qu: Where could your idea be better, and where do existing solutions have the edge?
general/konkurencja/porownaj/przewagi.he: An honest answer to the second part matters more than to the first.
general/konkurencja/dlaczego-zmiana/co-p: What would make someone choose your solution over their current way of doing things?
general/konkurencja/dlaczego-zmiana/co-u: What would make that switch hard?
Cost, moving data, learning to use it, habit, a manager's approval.
general/konkurencja/brak-konkurencji.tit: If you can't find similar solutions
general/konkurencja/brak-konkurencji.des: Fill this in only if you really found nothing. No competition more often means no market than an open field.
general/konkurencja/brak-konkurencji/pot: I haven't found similar solutions — I'm marking this deliberately.
Ticking this completes the remaining sub-points of this point without answers. If you find competition later, untick this field and fill them in.
general/konkurencja/brak-konkurencji/gdz: Which places have already been searched?
general/konkurencja/brak-konkurencji/dla: Why might such solutions not exist?
Consider whether the problem is unimportant, the solution hard to build or hard to make money on. It's also possible nobody has seized this opportunity yet.
general/konkurencja/brak-konkurencji/jak: How will you check your explanation?
general/zainteresowanie-i-cena.title: Check interest in the idea and the price
general/zainteresowanie-i-cena.guide_bod:
In this point you'll show a specific offer and ask for a small next step. You'll learn what people understand, what reservations they have and whether they want to give their attention or time to further contact. The price will be an initial proposal for discussion.
Prepare the offer and work out who pays
Use the solution description from point 2, improved after the interviews. A few sentences, a simple drawing or a demo of a sample result are enough. Say what already works and what you're only planning. At this stage you don't need a presentation with a full list of future features.
Example: “We're preparing a tool that turns a shop's files into a list of products to reorder. We want to check whether it will help you plan deliveries faster. For now we're showing a sample list”.
Work out who uses the solution and who decides on spending the money. An employee may use the tool while the shop owner pays for it. Write down these roles and try to talk to the person who decides on the purchase as well.
Give a specific price
Pick the first amount based on the comparison from point 3 and what you've learned about the current way of doing things. Say what the customer would pay for and how often. Example: “We're considering $12 a month for one shop and a weekly order list”. It's a made-up price to show how to phrase an offer.
You don't have to work out the ideal price or build a detailed forecast now. The chosen amount is for the conversation. If you change it later, note who was shown which version. The cost of preparing the product and the cost of serving the customer will still need separate checking.
Decide on the action and the result before the test
Ask for a step you can observe: signing up for tests or booking a short meeting with a specific date. Pick a step you can handle right away. The answer “sounds interesting” alone doesn't count as taking that action.
Write down whom you'll show the offer to, how many people, by when and what result will make you keep checking. An example working rule: “Within a week I'll present the same offer to five shop owners. If two of them book a test date, I'll prepare it for them”. This threshold serves a small decision in the example. It isn't a norm for other ideas or proof of demand for the product.
If the test is free, write that down. Signing up for it shows interest in a free test. Note the reaction to the future price separately.
Present the idea and write down what happened
You can go back to the people from point 4. Show each of them a comparable description and a clearly stated price. Ask how they understand the offer, what would be useful to them and what would stop them from using it. When you hear “too expensive”, follow up: “What are you comparing this amount with?” and “What raises the biggest doubt?”. Don't assume straight away that a discount is enough.
For each person note: the version of the offer and the price, the reaction, the reason for interest or refusal, the proposed step and the action taken. Separate “agreed to book” from “picked a date”, and later from “came to the meeting”.
Sum up the number of actions against the number of people who saw the offer, e.g. “2 of 5 booked a test”. Record no response as well, but don't attribute a made-up reason to it. If five people got the invitation and only two replied, keep both numbers. Don't present a free sign-up as a purchase.
Decide what you'll keep and what you'll check next
Go back to the assumption chosen in point 2 and judge whether the test you ran was about it at all. If the test was meant to check readiness to share files, a sign-up for a conversation doesn't yet answer that.
Base the decision on reasons and actions. If recipients describe the need and take the agreed step, you can prepare the next test. If they have the problem but don't understand the offer, improve the description and check it again. If they don't see a significant benefit or their current way is enough for them, consider changing the solution or the group. When the information is too thin, point out exactly what's missing.
The final note should say: what you've learned, what you're changing, what remains uncertain and what the next step will be. Example: “Two people booked a test, but neither has used the solution yet and neither has paid for it. I'll prepare sample lists for them and check whether they help with ordering”.
After this point you have the first reactions to the offer and the price, and a decision based on the information collected. This still doesn't prove that the product works, that customers will come back or that revenue will cover costs. You'll check those questions in the next steps of the work.
general/zainteresowanie-i-cena.guide_sou: Michael Seibel, The Real Product Market Fit. Basis: caution in declaring success and continued learning from product use.
Michael Seibel, How to Plan an MVP. Basis: moving to a simple solution used by the first recipients. The link leads to a summary and a recording of the lecture.
Paul Graham, Do Things that Don't Scale. Basis: working directly with the first users.
"How to Get Startup Ideas" – Paul Graham / Jared Friedman
"Do Things that Don't Scale" – Paul Graham (the famous essay about doing things by hand at the start)
"How to Plan an MVP" – Michael Seibel (on ruthlessly cutting features and simplifying the product)
"How to Talk to Users" – Eric Migicovsky
"How to Get and Test Ideas" – Kevin Hale
general/zainteresowanie-i-cena/propozycj: What do you offer and how will it help the person you're talking to?
Above the field you have the problem definition, your hypothesis and the minimum version. Summarize from them what you offer — two sentences at most.
Who would pay, how much and for what?
$8 a month for using the app, paid by the shop owner.
general/zainteresowanie-i-cena/miara-zai: Decide this before you start talking — otherwise you'll always find a reason to call the result good.
What action will you ask for?
Something that takes effort: signing up for tests, booking another conversation, giving an email address, paying a deposit.
How many people will you present the offer to, and how many of them have to take this action for you to continue?
I'll present it to 15 people and continue if at least 4 sign up for tests.
general/zainteresowanie-i-cena/przedstaw: Present the idea and the price
Talk to a few people affected by the problem. If someone other than the user is meant to pay, talk to them too.
How did the people you talked to rate the idea and the price? What convinced them, and what put them off?
How many people took the proposed action out of everyone the idea was presented to?
Praise for the idea, a sign-up for free tests and the statement “I'd pay” mean different things. None of them on its own proves that someone will buy.
general/zainteresowanie-i-cena/decyzja/w: What will you keep, what will you change and what do you still need to check?
This is the summary of the whole stage. In a month you'll come back to it and check whether the plan was kept.
saas.title: SaaS
saas.intro: A subscription makes sense when the problem comes back regularly — so often that the customer renews every month or every year. Check how often the problem comes back, how long getting started takes, what will keep the customer and what will put them off.
saas/za-co-placi.title: What the customer will pay for while using it
saas/za-co-placi.description: Use the problem description and the price proposal from General validation. Here you'll check whether the way fees are charged fits how the program is used.
saas/za-co-placi.guide_body:
Define what the program provides over time
The general part already describes the main benefit. Now think about what the customer will get after the first use and why they will still need the program.
The program can handle further tasks, store information, enable collaboration or keep doing work in the background. For example, a booking tool accepts the next bookings, and a backup program protects further versions of files.
How often the program is opened doesn't always show how useful it is. A user may rarely look at a tool that constantly keeps an eye on something for them. So describe what the person does and what the program provides between their visits.
Then work out how long the customer needs this help. Someone running regular classes may use a booking program all year. The organizer of a single event may need it for a few months. Someone converting files may come back only for specific tasks.
Go back to the examples from earlier conversations. Check when the need last came up, how often it came back and when it ended. If you don't have this information yet, write down an assumption to check.
Avoid the answer “the customer will come back thanks to notifications”. A notification can remind someone of a task, but you still have to explain why doing that task is needed.
Match the way fees are charged
Choose what the customer will pay for. It can be a month of access, the number of people using it or the number of tasks done. Match the billing method to how the program is used.
With a per-user fee, explain whom you count: every person with an account, a team member or a person actively using it. With a usage fee, define what one use is, e.g. processing one document.
Then list what the price given in the general part includes. Instead of “$12 for the program” you can write: “$12 a month for a booking calendar for one person, up to 100 bookings a month”. This is an example of how to describe an offer, not a suggested price.
Include the program's main capabilities and significant limits in the list. If you plan a limit, explain what happens when it's exceeded. The customer should understand how their bill will come about.
You don't need to create several plans now. One clear offer is enough for the first check.
Check the reaction to the billing method
Present the price to the person you're talking to together with the rule for charging fees. Ask what suits them, what bothers them and how such billing would fit the way they'd use it.
You can ask:
“How do you currently pay for similar tools?”
“Does the number of tasks you do change a lot from month to month?”
“What would be unclear to you about charging fees this way?”
“Which paid program have you recently cancelled? Why?”
If someone rejects a subscription, check the reason. It may be the price, occasional use, the length of the commitment or an insufficient benefit. Don't assume straight away that lowering the amount is enough.
Also ask when the person would stop needing your solution. The need may end with a project, a job change or a switch to another tool. Write these situations down as possible reasons for cancelling.
Separate experiences from predictions. “I cancelled the program because I only needed it for one event” describes an event. “I'd use your program all year” remains a statement.
After this point you have an initial way of charging fees, a description of what the price covers and the comments of the people you talked to. You'll only check payment renewals while the product is being used.
saas/za-co-placi.guide_sources.0: Kevin Hale, How to Evaluate Startup Ideas. Recognizing the need and the assumptions the idea's success depends on. A summary and a recording of the lecture at YC.
saas/za-co-placi.guide_sources.1: Eric Migicovsky, How to Talk to Users. Asking about specific experiences and the current way of doing things. A summary and a recording of the lecture at YC.
saas/za-co-placi/co-zapewnia-z-czasem.ti: Define what the program provides over time
saas/za-co-placi/co-zapewnia-z-czasem/po: What will the customer get right after the first use?
E.g. handling further orders, storing data, teamwork or constant monitoring.
saas/za-co-placi/co-zapewnia-z-czasem/ro: Does the customer need constant access, use for a set period, or only individual tasks done?
You can base the answer on examples from the conversations in General validation. This decides whether a subscription makes sense at all.
saas/za-co-placi/sposob-naliczania.title: Match the way fees are charged
saas/za-co-placi/sposob-naliczania/za-co: What do you want to charge for?
E.g. a month of access, the number of users or the number of tasks done.
saas/za-co-placi/sposob-naliczania/w-cen: What will the customer get for the price given in General validation?
Check the reaction to the billing method
If there have already been conversations with people about this problem, go back to the same people — you don't need to look for new ones.
saas/za-co-placi/reakcja-na-rozliczenie/: What do the people you asked like, and what bothers them, about charging fees this way?
In what case might they stop needing paid access or cut back on using it?
These are future reasons for cancelling. Better to learn them now than after a year.
saas/start-korzystania.title: Check whether the customer will be able to start using it
saas/start-korzystania.description: Work out what has to be available for the program to help anyone. At this stage it's enough to recognize the obstacles and the unknowns.
saas/start-korzystania.guide_body:
What the program needs to start
Imagine a person who wants to get the promised benefit for the first time. Think about what they have to prepare beforehand: files, data, access to other tools or settings.
List only the things needed for the main action. An order-planning program may need a product list, sales information and current stock. A booking program may require entering availability hours and the kind of services offered.
For each item, work out where the user will get it. Do they already have it in another program? Do they have to prepare it by hand? Do they need someone else's help or permission?
Don't assume that being able to view information means being able to download and pass it on. Ask how the user would do it with their current way of working.
Treat the question about whether sharing the data is legal as a place for findings and matters that need clarifying. Write down:
What kind of information is to go into the program.
Whom it comes from and whether it concerns other people.
In which countries you plan to offer the service.
What restrictions the customer or the provider of the tool they use has mentioned.
If you can't assess the situation, write down the specific unknown and the person who will help clarify it. Example: “To check with the person responsible for data protection: can the shop hand over a file containing information about its customers”.
YC materials don't settle legal questions. Clarify doubts about the legality of using the data with a suitable specialist before using that data in a test. To discuss the idea, you can prepare a made-up sample file.
Check the connections to other programs you need
An “integration” is a connection that lets programs work together. For example, a new booking can automatically appear in the user's calendar.
List the connections you need and for each explain what information is to be passed and why. Instead of just “calendar connection” write: “fetching busy slots, so as not to offer a visit at an unavailable time”.
Focus on the connections needed to deliver the main promise. Don't add every popular program someone might use.
Then check whether a simpler way of passing information will do at the start. An automatic connection can sometimes be replaced by sending a file. CSV is a simple format for tabular data. What matters is whether the current program lets you export the needed information in this or another usable format.
Look at the program's instructions or ask its support. If you need a developer's help, show them specifically: what data, from where, to where and how often it should go.
Ask the user what sending a file by hand would look like in their work. Preparing the data once may be acceptable. Repeating it a dozen times a day may make the solution pointless.
If the main promise requires information to be updated instantly, sending files by hand may not be enough. Write this limitation down as something to solve.
Write down the conditions for starting to use it
Collect the obstacles that could stop a user before the first use. They may concern preparing data, difficult settings, no access to a needed program or concerns about storing information in a new place.
Phrase them specifically. “Lack of trust” explains little. “The interviewee doesn't want to send documents until they know who will have access to them” points to a question that needs answering.
For each obstacle, mark whether the interviewee named it or whether it's your assumption. Add a way to check it: another conversation, looking at the instructions, a question to the program's provider or a technical consultation.
You don't have to remove every obstacle right away. At this stage, above all work out which of them could make the main promise impossible to deliver and need clarifying before further work.
After this point you have a list of things needed to start using it, the necessary connections and the obstacles. You know what has been checked and what remains unknown.
saas/start-korzystania.guide_sources.0: Paul Graham, Do Things that Don’t Scale. Personal help for the first users and doing part of the work by hand at the start. Source text.
saas/start-korzystania.guide_sources.1: Geoff Ralston, YC’s Essential Startup Advice. Looking for a simple way to deliver the basic benefit without expanding the product too early. Source text.
saas/start-korzystania.guide_sources.2: The instructions on data and connections between programs are an extension of the Vairo exercise. Assessing a specific connection requires the documentation of the tool in question, and a legal assessment of the data requires a separate check.
What the program needs to start
saas/start-korzystania/czego-potrzebuje/: What data, files, access or settings are needed before the first use?
If none — write “nothing is needed”. That's very good news for your product.
Where will the user get them and can they share them?
Is sharing this data legal? If so, on what basis?
Personal data, customer data, financial data — this is where the real obstacles start, the ones that are easy to forget.
saas/start-korzystania/integracje.title: Check the connections to other programs you need
saas/start-korzystania/integracje/z-czym: Which programs does your solution have to exchange data with to deliver the main promise?
If none — write “none”. Every integration is weeks of work, so it's better to know for sure.
saas/start-korzystania/integracje/prosts: Will a simpler way, e.g. sending a file, be enough at the start? Do those programs allow it at all?
saas/start-korzystania/warunki-startu.ti: Write down the conditions for starting to use it
saas/start-korzystania/warunki-startu/co: What could stop the customer from using an online program or storing data in it?
saas/start-korzystania/warunki-startu/po: Which of these obstacles did the interviewees name, and which still need checking?
Add next to each: “the interviewee said” or “my guess”. Guesses are for checking, not for planning.
saas/jeden-program-rozni-klienci.title: Check whether one program can serve different customers
saas/jeden-program-rozni-klienci.descrip: Compare the needs of the people you talked to. Check whether you can offer them a shared product and what help they will need.
saas/jeden-program-rozni-klienci.guide_b:
Separate shared needs from individual wishes
Go back to your interview notes. Compare what individual people are trying to achieve and what actions are needed for it. Look for a shared task your program can handle in a similar way.
A tutor, a coach and a music teacher may need to set free slots, take bookings and send class reminders. At the same time, each may have extra expectations related to their work.
Next to shared needs, add which interviewees raised them. List the wishes of individual people separately. This makes it easier to notice whether you're expanding the main idea or starting to build a separate product for one customer.
Different expectations don't always require separate versions of the program. Visit length, service name and availability hours can be settings. A bigger difference appears when the customer needs a different way of working, e.g. scheduling dozens of employees instead of booking individual classes.
With an unusual wish, ask what problem it is meant to solve. Check whether a similar need came up for other people and whether it fits within the program's main promise.
You don't have to serve all groups from the start. If the needs clearly diverge, you can narrow the group of first customers.
Define the help needed
Write down what has to be prepared separately for each customer. It may be moving data, setting up an account, connecting a calendar or explaining how to use it.
Then describe the help needed later. Separate one-off tasks from those that will recur.
Example:
At the start you help the user enter services and set availability.
Later the user handles bookings themselves.
When their way of working changes, they may need the settings explained.
Such a description shows who does the work and when. A general “the customer will need support” doesn't give enough information yet.
At the start you can help in person. This way you'll learn about users' difficulties and see which tasks are worth simplifying. But mark whether the help is meant to be temporary or will remain a permanent part of the service.
You don't have to price every task precisely now. Above all, point out the duties that may regularly take a lot of time or require a separate approach for each customer.
Name the biggest unknown
Go through the expectations and the help needed. Consider whether any of them means building a separate version of the program or permanently doing work for the customer.
The mere existence of such a need doesn't rule the idea out. But you need to know whether it concerns one person or most of the chosen recipients, and how it affects the scope of the service offered.
Pick the matter that most needs clarifying before building. It could be:
Uncertainty about whether customers provide data in a similar format.
Every interviewee expecting different features.
The need to regularly fix data for the user.
A big difference between the needs of the groups you want to serve.
Add what you'll check and with whom. For example: “I'll compare the interviewees' sample files and ask a developer whether they can be handled with one way of importing”.
Avoid a general “I have to check whether it can be done”. Phrase a question a specific person can answer. If you don't know whether an expectation matters to the customer at all, go back to the interviewee. If you don't know how it will affect building the program, talk to a technical person.
After this point you have a description of the shared part of the product, a list of individual expectations and a picture of the help needed. You also know which unknown needs clarifying first.
saas/jeden-program-rozni-klienci.guide_s: Paul Graham, Do Things that Don’t Scale. Learning by working directly with the first customers before all tasks are automated. Source text.
Geoff Ralston, YC’s Essential Startup Advice. Limiting scope, choosing customers deliberately and avoiding expanding the product for every request that comes up. Source text.
Eric Migicovsky, How to Talk to Users. Understanding the problem behind a feature request. A summary and a recording of the lecture at YC.
saas/jeden-program-rozni-klienci/wspolne: Separate shared needs from individual wishes
What should the program do the same way for most of the first customers?
This is your actual product. The rest are options.
What changes or add-ons do only individual interviewees expect?
saas/jeden-program-rozni-klienci/potrzeb: What will have to be prepared or set up separately for each customer?
The longer this list, the harder it is to serve the tenth customer as well as the first.
What help might the customer need later?
E.g. when changing settings, data or the way of working.
saas/jeden-program-rozni-klienci/najwiek: Does any expectation require a separate version of the program or regularly doing work for the customer?
If so, it's no longer SaaS but a service. That doesn't have to be bad news — but you need to know it.
What do you need to clarify before you start building, and with whom will you check it?
b2b.title: B2B
b2b.intro: You're selling to companies. The person who uses it usually doesn't decide: the employee wants a better tool, but the boss gives the approval. Work out whom in the company you're helping, who approves the purchase and what has to happen for the company to start using it.
b2b/decyzja-o-zakupie.title: Check how the customer decides to buy
b2b/decyzja-o-zakupie.guide_body:
Describe the target company and the user in the company
Start with the profile prepared earlier. Add the traits that matter for the purchase: what the company does, how big it is and in what situation it needs your help.
A sample description could be: "A catering company with 10 to 30 employees that prepares meals for several offices every day and has trouble keeping track of container returns". Such a description helps you choose the companies worth contacting.
Then name the person who will use the solution. Describe their duties and the way of working related to the problem. In the catering example, it could be the person who hands meals to the drivers and takes back the containers.
You don't need to know a specific employee's name. The role is enough to start with. In a small company, the user and the buyer may be the owner themselves.
Who decides on the purchase
Assign roles to the people involved in the purchase: who feels the problem, who can allocate money to a solution, who approves the purchase and who signs the contract. Also mark who might raise objections.
One person can hold several of these roles. Don't add more positions just to fill the list.
Distinguishing the user from the person who decides on the spending is important: an employee may need help but not be able to order a solution. Both Eric Migicovsky and the authors of the study on B2B startups point this out.
During the conversation you can ask: "The last time you bought something similar, who took part in the decision?".
Check the approvals required
First name the department or person you want to help. Then work out whether the purchase has to be checked by someone else as well.
For example: equipment is bought by the warehouse manager, but a larger expense is approved by the owner. A service is ordered by marketing, and the contract wording is checked by a lawyer. The department using the solution and the department checking the purchase may be different.
IT, finance or the legal department mentioned in the task are examples. Don't assume that every company has such departments or that every purchase needs their approval.
For each approval needed, add briefly what it concerns. "The owner's approval of the expense" says more than just "the owner".
The purchasing path
Put the actions you've learned about in order. A short list describing how the company goes from noticing the need to using the purchase is enough.
Example for warehouse equipment:
The manager notices that the current equipment slows down packing.
They look for a suitable solution and compare offers.
The owner approves the expense.
The company places the order and arranges delivery.
Employees start using the equipment.
If your offer includes ongoing cooperation, add the moment of the decision to continue it. With a one-off purchase there may be no contract renewal.
The names of the steps are enough here. You'll describe waiting times in point 2, and the preparations after the purchase in point 4.
b2b/decyzja-o-zakupie.guide_sources.0: Brecht et al., Discovery and Validation of Business Models: How B2B Startups can use Business Experiments, especially the distinction between the user and the decision-maker.
b2b/decyzja-o-zakupie.guide_sources.1: Eric Migicovsky, How to Talk to Users, especially the questions about past experiences and the ability to approve spending.
b2b/decyzja-o-zakupie/docelowa-firma.tit: Describe the target company and the user
b2b/decyzja-o-zakupie/docelowa-firma/pro: Describe the ideal customer profile — the company.
Industry, size, number of employees, way of working, technological maturity. The narrower, the easier it is to find.
Describe the person who will use your solution.
Role, situation, industry — whatever matters for your idea. If the answer was already given in General validation, you'll see your answer here.
b2b/decyzja-o-zakupie/kto-decyduje.title: Who decides on the purchase
Who has the problem, who controls the budget, who signs the contract, and who can block the purchase?
Write one role per item. Often these are four different people — and each needs a different argument.
b2b/decyzja-o-zakupie/wymagane-zgody/dzi: Which departments do you have to reach?
E.g. IT, legal, security, finance. Each of them can hold up a purchase for weeks.
b2b/decyzja-o-zakupie/wymagane-zgody/dod: Is approval needed from anyone else?
b2b/decyzja-o-zakupie/sciezka-zakupowa/k: Lay out the process from the moment the problem appears to the decision, and then to use and contract renewal.
One item is one step. You'll see how many things have to happen before anyone pays.
b2b/czas-sprzedazy.title: Examine the timing and conditions of the sales process
b2b/czas-sprzedazy.guide_body:
Check how the company decides to buy
Go back to the list of people and approvals from point 1. Now work out when the company can make a decision and allocate money to the purchase.
A budget is money planned for specific expenses. The company may already have funds for a similar purchase or may need to include it in its next plans. Don't assume in advance that it has to wait until next year.
A helpful question is: "What did the last similar purchase look like, and how much time passed from reporting the need to placing the order?". Asking about a specific situation is in line with Migicovsky’s approach to talking to users.
If you're researching on your own, check the chosen company's information for suppliers, requests for quotes and procurement notices. They may contain deadlines or requirements. If there's no such information, it has to be found out another way.
Write down an approximate time if you have something to base it on. You can also say what it depends on, e.g. "the owner approves small purchases right away; larger expenses are discussed once a month".
Identify the biggest delays
Go through the purchasing path and mark the places where the company may wait for the next step. Examples are checking the contract, collecting several offers, ending current cooperation or finding time for a test.
Be specific: "The purchase is waiting for three offers to be compared". Just "procedures" doesn't explain what has to be done or where the delay arises.
During the conversation, ask what held up the previous similar purchase. Separate an obstacle that only lengthens the wait from a condition without which the company won't buy at all.
Finally, write down what this means for your idea. If the chosen companies need several months to decide, take that into account in your plan for winning the first customers.
b2b/czas-sprzedazy.guide_sources.0: Eric Migicovsky, How to Talk to Users, principles for collecting information about past events.
b2b/czas-sprzedazy.guide_sources.1: Gustaf Alströmer, How to Get Your First Customers, material on the beginnings of sales and winning customers. The detailed questions about deadlines and approvals are an adaptation to the Vairo tasks.
b2b/czas-sprzedazy/jak-decyduje.title: Check how the company decides
b2b/czas-sprzedazy/jak-decyduje/ile-osob: Is one person's decision enough, or is approval from several needed?
b2b/czas-sprzedazy/jak-decyduje/budzet.q: Can the company buy such a solution at any time, or does it have to plan the money for it in advance?
b2b/czas-sprzedazy/jak-decyduje/budzet.h: A planned budget means the sale may have to wait until next year.
b2b/czas-sprzedazy/opoznienia.title: Identify the biggest delays
Holidays, a security audit, the legal department, the end of the financial year, a change of the person in the role.
b2b/roi.title: Check whether the purchase pays off for the company
b2b/roi.description: ROI (Return On Investment) is a simple answer to the question: will it pay off for the company. You don't need a spreadsheet — an honest estimate is enough.
b2b/roi.guide_body:
How much the problem costs the customer
Use the information from the general part. Complete it so that the current situation can be compared with the expected improvement.
Pick one period, e.g. a month. Write down how much time the company spends on the problem, what expenses it incurs and how many mistakes occur. For mistakes, also explain their effects: an extra delivery, fixing an order, wasted materials.
Example: "In a month the company sends about 20 parcels with a mistake. Resending costs an average of $6 per parcel, about $120 in total".
If you only have the interviewee's estimates, mark that. When amounts are missing, leave the number of hours or mistakes and add what else you need to calculate the cost.
Migicovsky suggests asking about the current cost of the problem and the available budget. Hale points to a costly or urgent problem as one of the reasons a solution may be needed.
Convert the benefits into money and compare them with the price
Take the price from the general part. Then estimate what share of the current cost your solution can reduce. Don't automatically assume it will remove all losses.
In the parcel example, you can assume for checking that the number of mistakes will drop by half. That would mean saving about $60 a month on resending. If the solution costs $35 a month, the difference is $25 before other costs are taken into account.
Compare the same period. With a one-off purchase, you can check after how many months the expected savings will cover the expense. Include the known costs of starting to use it, e.g. preparing a workstation or training.
Watch out for two common mistakes:
Time saved doesn't always mean lower spending. An employee may use it for other tasks while getting the same salary.
Don't count the same benefit twice. If the cost of fixing mistakes already includes the employee's work, don't add it again as a separate saving.
Ask the person who decides on the purchase what result would justify the expense and how long the company can wait for it. Write it down as an expectation to check in a later test.
Include the soft benefits
"Soft benefits" are advantages that are hard to put a specific amount on. Describe how they will change daily work.
Instead of "more convenience" you can write: "Employees check the order status in one place and don't have to call the warehouse". Instead of "less stress": "The person responsible for deliveries sees missing products earlier".
Don't make up a monetary value just to make the calculation look better. Mark who named the benefit and whether it matters to the person approving the purchase.
b2b/roi.guide_sources.0: Eric Migicovsky, How to Talk to Users, and Kevin Hale, How to Evaluate Startup Ideas, Y Combinator materials and transcript.
b2b/roi.guide_sources.1: Brecht et al., Discovery and Validation of Business Models: How B2B Startups can use Business Experiments, studying customers' tasks, the time spent and the costs. The calculation example is an illustration prepared for this guide.
b2b/roi/koszt-problemu.title: How much the problem costs the customer
b2b/roi/koszt-problemu/czas.question: How much time does the problem cost them today?
b2b/roi/koszt-problemu/czas.example: About 6 hours a week, two people.
b2b/roi/koszt-problemu/pieniadze.questio: How much money does the problem cost them today?
b2b/roi/koszt-problemu/bledy.question: How many mistakes or losses does this problem cause?
b2b/roi/przelicz-na-pieniadze.title: Convert the benefits into money and compare them with the price
b2b/roi/przelicz-na-pieniadze/cena.quest: What price will the customer pay for your solution?
b2b/roi/przelicz-na-pieniadze/minimalny-: What minimum result, and in what time, will persuade them to buy?
“It has to pay for itself within six months” is a typical answer. Learn it before the price conversation.
b2b/roi/korzysci-miekkie.title: Include the soft benefits
b2b/roi/korzysci-miekkie/lista.question: Write down the advantages that are harder to put a number on.
b2b/roi/korzysci-miekkie/lista.help: Comfort at work, less stress for the team, lower risk, a better image. On their own they won't close a sale, but they often tip the balance.
b2b/po-zakupie.title: Check what the company needs after the purchase
b2b/po-zakupie.description: The sale isn't the end. If nobody starts using it after the contract is signed, the contract won't be renewed.
b2b/po-zakupie.guide_body:
Work out what the company has to prepare
In this conversation, move on to the situation after the purchase. Work out what has to be prepared before employees start using the product or service.
For a device, it may be a place and a suitable power supply. For a catalog preparation service: photos, product descriptions and a person who approves the content. For training: a date and the employees' availability.
Assign a person on the company's side to each preparation. Also mark what the company wants to do itself and what it expects from you.
At the idea stage it's enough to recognize the most important conditions for starting work. If data or connections between programs are already described in the SaaS part, refer to that answer and add the customer's duties to it.
Check what help employees need
Work out what will change in the work of the people using the solution. Will a short instruction be enough, or will a new way of doing the task have to be shown?
Help at the start may include a demonstration, setting up equipment or doing the first task together. Later help may concern breakdowns, new employees or changes in how it's used.
Ask what general expectations mean. If the interviewee says "we need support", ask for an example of a situation in which they'll need it.
Write down who needs help, with what, and whether it will be a one-off or a recurring task. This will later let you define the scope of customer service.
Work out what can make using it difficult
Talk about what could stop employees from adopting the new way of working. A question about an earlier purchase the company rarely used or gave up entirely will help.
Ask for a description of the reason. Was there no time to learn? Did the solution add duties? Did the person responsible for getting it started leave the company?
In the study by Brecht et al., the conversations revealed, among other things, the problem of entering information into several systems. This is an example of an obstacle that can be missed when focusing only on product features.
For each difficulty named, write down whether it comes from the company's earlier experience or is a concern about your idea. Pick the most important obstacle to clarify before building or the first test.
If you don't have an interviewee yet, write down the questions and the person worth reaching with them. You can use the conversations held in the general part and add these topics to them.
b2b/po-zakupie.guide_sources.0: Brecht et al., Discovery and Validation of Business Models: How B2B Startups can use Business Experiments, especially the conclusions on fitting the solution to the customer's existing work.
b2b/po-zakupie.guide_sources.1: Eric Migicovsky, How to Talk to Users, questions about past experiences and difficulties with existing solutions.
b2b/po-zakupie/przygotowanie.title: Work out what the company has to prepare
b2b/po-zakupie/przygotowanie/co-musi-sie: What has to happen between the purchase and starting to use it?
E.g. preparing a place, handing over materials or changing the way of working.
b2b/po-zakupie/przygotowanie/kto-sie-zaj: Who in the company will take care of this preparation?
b2b/po-zakupie/pomoc-pracownikow.title: Check what help employees need
b2b/po-zakupie/pomoc-pracownikow/czego-s: What will they have to learn to use the solution?
b2b/po-zakupie/pomoc-pracownikow/jaka-po: What help do they expect from you at the start, and what later?
b2b/po-zakupie/co-utrudni.title: Work out what can make using it difficult
b2b/po-zakupie/co-utrudni/powroty-do-sta: What could make employees stick with the old way of working despite the purchase?
No time to learn, having to do the same thing twice, habit, no support from the boss.
b2b/po-zakupie/co-utrudni/poprzednie-zak: Has the company bought something similar before that then went unused? If so, why?
This is the most valuable question in the whole point. The answer tells you what to avoid.
b2c.title: B2C
b2c.intro: In the B2C model, the solution serves private individuals or households. Specify who takes part in the purchase, in what situation they decide on it and what private funds they pay for it from. Treat information that isn't confirmed yet as assumptions.
b2c/zakup-konsumencki.title: Specify the consumer purchase
b2c/zakup-konsumencki.guide_body:
Work out who uses it, who chooses and who pays
When buying for oneself, one person can hold all the roles. A purchase for a child, as a gift or for a shared home can involve several people, and their expectations may differ. Lay out only the roles that occur in the chosen situation.
Example: a final-exam prep course. The student uses it, the student chooses together with a parent, the parent pays. The student may be looking for clear explanations, while the parent pays attention to exam preparation and cost. With a gift, the payer is the buyer and the user is the person receiving it.
Name the occasion for the purchase
Use the recipient defined earlier and describe the specific moment when your idea may become useful to them. The occasion for a purchase can be falling behind before final exams, a loved one's birthday or a new need appearing at home.
An example assumption: a parent looks for a course when the student starts having trouble preparing for final exams. With a gift, the moment of purchase may come a few weeks before use. One sentence about the chosen situation is enough.
Place the expense in the private budget
Specify where in the private budget the money for the purchase is to come from. For an exam prep course it may be the child's education, and for a gift the amount set aside for a specific occasion. Use the alternatives described earlier to determine whether the purchase replaces a current expense.
An example entry: the child's education; the course replaces part of the spending on private tutoring. If the existing solution was free, the new fee will be an extra burden on the budget. The entry remains an assumption to be checked later. In the free variant, mark that there's no fee for the consumer and skip the remaining fields of this sub-point.
b2c/zakup-konsumencki/role-zakupu.title: Work out who uses it, who chooses and who pays
b2c/zakup-konsumencki/role-zakupu.descri: Mark whom the purchase is for and assign the roles. If the same person holds all of them, one tick is enough.
b2c/zakup-konsumencki/role-zakupu/jedna-: The same person uses it, chooses and pays.
b2c/zakup-konsumencki/role-zakupu/wybier: e.g. the student together with a parent
b2c/zakup-konsumencki/okazja-zakupu.titl: Name the occasion for the purchase
b2c/zakup-konsumencki/okazja-zakupu.desc: One situation from private life in which the consumer will consider buying — e.g. starting a hobby, preparing for an exam or choosing a gift.
b2c/zakup-konsumencki/okazja-zakupu/sytu: In what situation will the consumer consider buying, and why does the expense make sense exactly then?
e.g. a parent looks for a course when the student starts having trouble preparing for final exams
b2c/zakup-konsumencki/prywatny-budzet.ti: Place the expense in the private budget
b2c/zakup-konsumencki/prywatny-budzet.de: Specify where in the private budget the money is to come from and whether the purchase replaces an existing expense.
b2c/zakup-konsumencki/prywatny-budzet/ro: How does the purchase fit into the consumer's budget?
b2c/zakup-konsumencki/prywatny-budzet/ka: What expense does it replace, or what category does it belong to?
e.g. the child's education; the course replaces part of the spending on private tutoring. Leave it empty for free access.
b2c/pozyskanie-klientow.title: How to find customers and what it costs
b2c/pozyskanie-klientow.guide_body:
Define who the product is for
First, define precisely whom you're aiming your product at. Try to describe your customer's characteristics in great detail. For example, if your idea were an innovative final-exam prep course, don't write "my customer is a secondary school student". Write "My customer is a secondary school student preparing for the advanced-level English final exam. I'm aiming the product at students who changed their learning path, have gaps or difficulties in learning and need to catch up in record time". It's important to know exactly who will use your solution. This makes it easier for you to find customers and your direct competition.
Find where your customers are
Think about the easiest way to reach the customer and where to win them. Today these are most often groups on social media, trade fairs, themed events or ads. Think about where your target group gets information, shares its thoughts and looks for solutions. Pinpointing this place is key to winning the customer and staying in touch with them.
Test a simple ad:
Create an ad about your product. Share it in a chosen social channel used by potential customers. See who is interested in your idea and how many users you can win. It doesn't have to be an ad for the final product. Customers themselves will tell you what they need and what will make your product stand out. Use their knowledge and feedback.
Calculate the cost of winning one customer:
Divide the amount of money spent on ads or promoting the post by the number of customers who said they wanted to use the product. In this sub-point you also include the marketing team's pay, the costs of email tools, etc. This tells you how much it costs you to win one customer. If your way of promoting didn't require extra funding, write that in the gap. The cheaper you win customers, the better. But remember that it's sometimes worth using paid ads, because they let you reach a wider audience.
Choose a way of advertising:
At the start, don't lock yourself into one way of advertising. Test different sources. This way you'll see where it pays best to win customers. After the testing phase, pick the source that gave the best results. Remember to keep one or two extra ones for the future.
b2c/pozyskanie-klientow/gdzie-sa-klienci: Find the places where your customers are
Exactly whom are you aiming the product at?
The narrower, the cheaper it is to find them. “Everyone” is the most expensive target group in the world.
Pick 3–5 places where they're easiest to reach.
E.g. Facebook groups, ads, trade fairs, themed forums, industry newsletters.
b2c/pozyskanie-klientow/test-ogloszenia/: I've put out a short piece of information about the product in the chosen places.
You don't need a product — a description of what you intend to make is enough.
Who was interested in your idea?
Who reacted, what did they ask, were they the people you had in mind?
How many people said they wanted to use it?
b2c/pozyskanie-klientow/koszt-klienta.ti: Calculate the cost of winning one customer
b2c/pozyskanie-klientow/koszt-klienta/wy: How much did reaching these people cost?
Ads, materials, trade fair tickets. If it cost nothing, enter 0.
b2c/pozyskanie-klientow/koszt-klienta/ca: How much did winning one interested person cost?
This is the cost of winning one customer (in the industry: CAC). Enter the amount spent and the number of interested people — the result calculates itself.
b2c/pozyskanie-klientow/koszt-klienta/cz: At this cost, does it pay off at all?
Compare it with the price you're planning. If winning a customer costs more than they will pay — you have a problem to solve now, not later.
b2c/pozyskanie-klientow/glowny-kanal.tit: Pick one main way of reaching people
b2c/pozyskanie-klientow/glowny-kanal/glo: Which place gave the best and cheapest results?
b2c/pozyskanie-klientow/glowny-kanal/zap: Which one are you keeping as a backup?
One channel is a risk. A second one in reserve costs little and saves you when the first stops working.
b2c/gotowosc-do-zaplaty.title: Assess willingness to pay
b2c/gotowosc-do-zaplaty.guide_body:
Separate the payer from the user, compare alternatives:
Find out who pays for the product and who uses it. Using our example of an innovative final-exam prep course: the payer may be a parent, and the user a student in the final year. This is one of the most important elements of running an effective business. Knowing who is who decides whether the product survives. The payer looks for business value, which is why in this point we also compare the cost of the alternatives payers currently use. The user looks for convenience, ease of use and a solution to the problem. This information will let you adjust, among other things, the product's marketing and its real value.
Collect and categorize the objections typical of individual purchases:
Estimate LTV (how much a customer will pay in total over the whole time they use it) and compare it with CAC (the cost of winning one customer):
LTV (Lifetime value) is the total revenue or profit a customer generates for the company over the whole cycle of cooperation. It's a measure of how profitable a customer is. It helps determine how much winning one user may cost.
The LTV formula:
LTV = Average order value * Average number of orders per year * Average length of cooperation
Example:
Average value of one order (one transaction) = $25
Average number of orders per year = 2 times
Average length of cooperation with the customer = 4 years
LTV = $25 * 2 * 4 = $200  (That's what the customer is worth over the period of cooperation.)
CAC is the average cost of winning one customer, calculated in point one. As a reminder: CAC = total marketing costs / number of customers won.
Finally, you divide LTV by CAC and enter the result in the gap.
b2c/gotowosc-do-zaplaty/obiekcje.title: Collect the objections and group them
b2c/gotowosc-do-zaplaty/obiekcje/lista.h: For each one, add where it comes from: lack of trust in the brand, no urgent need, or a comparison with an easily available alternative.
b2c/gotowosc-do-zaplaty/ltv-vs-cac.title: Estimate the customer's value and compare it with the cost
b2c/gotowosc-do-zaplaty/ltv-vs-cac/ltv.q: How much will the customer pay you in total over the whole time they use it?
b2c/gotowosc-do-zaplaty/ltv-vs-cac/ltv.h: This is the customer's value over the whole period of use (in the industry: LTV). Enter three numbers — the result calculates itself.
b2c/gotowosc-do-zaplaty/ltv-vs-cac/ltv.c: How many years they stay a customer
b2c/gotowosc-do-zaplaty/ltv-vs-cac/wnios: How does this amount compare with the cost of winning one customer from the point “How to find customers”?
The accepted rule says that what a customer pays in total should be several times higher than the cost of winning them. If it's the other way round, the business loses on every customer.
hardware.title: Hardware
hardware.intro: Check whether the device can be built and manufactured in a way that makes sense technically and financially. You're not building the finished product yet — you're catching the risks: feasibility, costs, time to market, demand and regulations.
hardware/problem-i-potrzeba-fizyczna.tit: Confirm the problem and the need for a physical device
hardware/problem-i-potrzeba-fizyczna.gui: Building a physical product requires validating technical feasibility, production costs, demand and compliance requirements before starting to build working prototypes. At the Idea Stage the process starts with interviewing potential users and making sure that the problem is real and that solving it requires a physical device rather than a simpler digital solution or a service. Next, a form concept (form factor) is created as sketches, 3D renders or simple cardboard or 3D-printed mock-ups (a looks-like model) to set the planned size, ergonomics and way of interacting, and it is then shown to customers to collect feedback and check whether they understand how the concept works.
The Hardware Startup" — Renee DiResta, Brady Forrest, and Ryan Vian
hardware/problem-i-potrzeba-fizyczna/dla: Justify the need to build hardware
Why does your solution require a physical device?
Make sure the problem can't be solved more simply — with just an app, a service or software. Hardware is an order of magnitude more expensive and slower.
hardware/problem-i-potrzeba-fizyczna/kon: What should the planned size, form and way of interacting with the product be?
Sketches, a 3D render or photos of a mock-up
A sketch or a render is enough — you don't have to build anything. A cardboard mock-up or a 3D print will also do.
hardware/problem-i-potrzeba-fizyczna/opi: Do potential customers understand how the device works and confirm they want to use it?
Show the sketch, render or mock-up without explaining. If you have to explain how it works — the form needs improving.
hardware/wykonalnosc-techniczna.title: Check initial technical feasibility
hardware/wykonalnosc-techniczna.guide_bo: After initially confirming the need for a physical product, the initial technical feasibility (High-Level Feasibility) should be assessed. To do this, list the key components (e.g. sensors, microcontrollers, batteries) needed to deliver the product's functions and verify their market availability and dimensions in their data sheets. The concept is discussed with an engineer (electronics or mechanical) to make sure that combining the parts in the intended enclosure is possible, and the part with the greatest technological risk is identified as the focus of further work.
hardware/wykonalnosc-techniczna.guide_so: The Hardware Startup" — Renee DiResta, Brady Forrest, and Ryan Vian
hardware/wykonalnosc-techniczna/technolo: Identify the key technologies and components
List the main parts needed for the product to work.
E.g. sensors, microcontrollers, batteries, motors, screens.
hardware/wykonalnosc-techniczna/dostepno: Verify the market availability of the technology
I've gone through the data sheets and confirmed that components with the needed parameters exist.
This is about parameters and dimensions, not just the category of the part.
Was there any component you couldn't find in the version you need?
hardware/wykonalnosc-techniczna/konsulta: Discuss the concept with an engineer
I've talked to a specialist (electronics or mechanical).
An hour's conversation can save half a year of work on something that won't work.
What did they say about combining these components in the intended enclosure?
hardware/wykonalnosc-techniczna/ryzyko-t: Which function is surrounded by the most uncertainty?
E.g. battery life, sensor precision, heat dissipation. This is what you'll deal with first.
hardware/koszty-jednostkowe.title: Estimate the unit costs
hardware/koszty-jednostkowe.description: A BOM (Bill of Materials) is a list of parts with prices. At this stage an estimate from a distributor is enough.
hardware/koszty-jednostkowe.guide_body: The next area is a rough analysis of unit costs (Rough BOM). Instead of a detailed supply chain, at this stage an initial list of parts is built from the retail prices of components at electronics distributors. To estimate the unit cost, the value of the components is multiplied by an assumed factor (e.g. 2x or 3x), taking into account the approximate cost of the enclosure, assembly, packaging and losses. The result is set against the expected selling price, checking the margin and identifying the components that create the greatest cost risk.
hardware/koszty-jednostkowe.guide_source: The Hardware Startup" — Renee DiResta, Brady Forrest, and Ryan Vian
hardware/koszty-jednostkowe/bom.title: Build an initial list of parts
hardware/koszty-jednostkowe/bom/czesci.q: List the known components with their retail prices.
hardware/koszty-jednostkowe/bom/arkusz.q: A spreadsheet with the cost breakdown
hardware/koszty-jednostkowe/koszt-jednos: How much do the components alone cost?
What will the unit cost come to after including the enclosure, assembly, packaging and losses?
Multiply the value of the components by 2 or 3. It's an approximation, but better than nothing.
hardware/koszty-jednostkowe/ryzyko-koszt: A price increase of which component would most threaten profitability?
E.g. a custom display, an expensive battery, an enclosure requiring an injection mold.
hardware/koszty-jednostkowe/koszt-vs-cen: Set the cost against the potential price
What selling price are you assuming?
Does the assumed margin allow the project to develop profitably?
In hardware it has to cover production, storage, shipping, returns, service and distribution.
hardware/zamiar-zakupu.title: Examine purchase intent
hardware/zamiar-zakupu.guide_body: In parallel, purchase intent, the value proposition and the early customer segment are validated. During the interviews, price acceptance of the presented mock-up or sketch is examined, and a group of early adopters for whom the problem is most acute is selected. Demand is measured not only through statements but above all through indicators of market engagement, such as waiting-list sign-ups, purchase intent on a landing page or pre-order forms.
hardware/zamiar-zakupu.guide_sources.1: The Hardware Startup" — Renee DiResta, Brady Forrest, and Ryan Vian
hardware/zamiar-zakupu/akceptacja-cenowa: What price range do potential users give?
Ask with the mock-up or sketch in front of them, not detached from the product.
How did they react to the price you're assuming?
hardware/zamiar-zakupu/testy-zaangazowan: In what form was market readiness checked?
A waiting-list sign-up, a purchase statement on a website, a pre-order form.
How many people took this action?
hardware/zamiar-zakupu/early-adopters/se: Who feels the problem most strongly, and for whom will the first version of the device be enough?
A narrow group that will forgive imperfections because it badly needs a solution.
hardware/regulacje.title: Outline the regulations and the rollout risks
hardware/regulacje.guide_body: The last area is outlining the regulations and the rollout risks. The product's category should be determined (e.g. consumer electronics, medical equipment, food contact) and the key certificates and standards (e.g. CE, FCC, RoHS) that apply in the target markets should be identified along with their restrictions. Finally, the collected demand, the engineer's opinion, the cost estimates and the regulatory outline should be put together to make a formal decision on moving to the Preparation stage and starting work on a detailed specification.
hardware/regulacje.guide_sources.1: The Hardware Startup" — Renee DiResta, Brady Forrest, and Ryan Vian
hardware/regulacje/kategoryzacja.title: Identify the product category
hardware/regulacje/kategoryzacja/kategor: Which group does the device belong to?
This determines how many certifications you'll need and how long it will take.
hardware/regulacje/kategoryzacja/uzasadn: What is this assessment based on?
hardware/regulacje/certyfikaty.title: Name the key certificates and standards
hardware/regulacje/certyfikaty/lista.que: What mandatory markings apply in your target markets?
hardware/regulacje/certyfikaty/lista.hel: E.g. CE, FCC, RoHS. An initial review is enough.
hardware/regulacje/certyfikaty/ogranicze: What critical restrictions do they impose on the product?
hardware/regulacje/decyzja.title: Decide whether to move on
Put together the collected demand, the engineer's opinion and the cost estimates. Does the project justify moving on to a detailed specification?
This is the moment for an honest answer. Hardware forgives less than software — a mistake at this stage costs months and money.
